title: Et tu, Brute? — Shakespearean invention
description: The famous dying words 'Et tu, Brute?' ('You too, Brutus?') are a Shakespearean invention from his play Julius Caesar (1599, Act 3, Scene 1). They have no basis in ancient sources. Suetonius (Jul. 82.2) reports that some said Caesar spoke in Greek: 'καὶ σύ, τέκνον' ('you too, child?'), but he also records that others said Caesar said nothing. Plutarch (Caes. 66.6) says Caesar covered his face in silence when he saw Brutus among the attackers. Appian (BC 2.117) says Caesar was silent. The Shakespearean phrase has become the dominant cultural image but is entirely fictional.

title: The 'Noble Brutus' tradition vs. historical reality
description: Ancient and modern sources often present Brutus as the 'noblest Roman of them all' — a selfless tyrannicide motivated by pure republican principle. This characterization comes primarily from Plutarch (Brut. 1, 29) and is reinforced by Shakespeare. In reality, Brutus had complex political and personal motivations: he profited from Caesar's favors (praetorship, provincial appointment), had family connections to the anti-Caesarian cause (uncle Cato), and was personally pressured by Cassius. The 'noble' framing is a moralizing literary construct — Brutus himself issued the EID MAR coins celebrating the assassination, which suggests a political calculation about his public image. Modern scholars (Tempest 2017) argue for a more nuanced reading.

title: The ghost of Caesar at Philippi
description: Plutarch (Brut. 36.4-7) and Appian (BC 4.134) report that Brutus was visited by a phantom in his tent the night before Philippi, which said 'You shall see me at Philippi.' Valerius Maximus (1.7.7) also records the story. The vision reflects the literary and moralizing tradition of divine retribution for Caesar's murder and cannot be treated as a historical event. It may also be an ex-eventu story invented after Brutus's defeat.

title: Brutus's motives — caution against interpretive overstatement
description: Ancient sources attribute various motives to Brutus's participation in the assassination: republican principle (Plutarch), personal honor (the family tradition of overthrowing tyrants), philosophical conviction (Stoic opposition to tyranny), and political calculation (opposition to Caesar's autocracy). No single motive is verifiable. Claims about Brutus's 'ideology' or 'beliefs' beyond contemporary attested positions must be marked as interpretation unless directly supported by his own writings or contemporary testimony. His surviving letters to Cicero (ad Brut.) show pragmatic political thinking rather than ideological purity.
